::: {.oneline}
A field behaves as a classical wave only when its phase is sharp, and a sharp
phase is possible only if the number of photons is not.
:::

## Short answer

A classical field is a definite waveform, in the sense that at each moment it
has a definite strength and a definite point in its cycle. This second property,
the phase, is what makes interference, beats and antenna physics work.

In quantum mechanics the number of photons in a mode and the phase of that mode
are complementary, in the same way as position and momentum. If we pin one down,
the other spreads out. A state with exactly one photon, or with exactly a
thousand, therefore has a completely undetermined phase, and does not correspond
to any particular waveform at all.

The classical wave is thus not the state with many photons. It is the state that
gives up knowing how many, in exchange for knowing where in the cycle the field
is. A laser produces exactly such a state: the photon number fluctuates from
measurement to measurement, and the relative size of that fluctuation shrinks as
the beam becomes brighter. This is what makes a bright laser look classical, and
not the brightness by itself.

Bright light with no phase relationship, such as the light from a hot filament,
never becomes classical in this sense, however bright we make it. It has an
intensity, but not a waveform.

## Why it works this way

The two descriptions have to meet somewhere, and this is where they do. Counting
photons and describing waves are not competing pictures of one state, but sharp
descriptions of different states. Asking whether light really is a wave or a
particle is therefore asking which of the two the source happened to prepare.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## The algebra: coherent states

A coherent state is an eigenstate of the annihilation operator,
$\hat a\lvert\alpha\rangle = \alpha\lvert\alpha\rangle$, and expands over
number states as

$$
\lvert\alpha\rangle = e^{-|\alpha|^2/2}
\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \frac{\alpha^{n}}{\sqrt{n!}} \lvert n\rangle .
$$ {#eq-coherent-state}

Photon number is Poissonian with mean $\bar n = |\alpha|^2$, so the relative
number fluctuation is $\Delta n/\bar n = 1/\sqrt{\bar n}$ and shrinks with
brightness. The field expectation value oscillates as a classical wave of
amplitude $|\alpha|$ and phase $\arg\alpha$, and the number–phase uncertainty
relation $\Delta n\,\Delta\phi \gtrsim 1/2$ is saturated.

Thermal light has the same mean intensity but number fluctuations
$\Delta n^2 = \bar n^2 + \bar n$, which do not become relatively small at any
brightness, and no preferred phase at all.
:::

## Common confusions

- **"Classical means many photons."** This is necessary but not sufficient,
  since a thermal source with the same photon flux as a laser is not a classical
  field.
- **"A coherent state has an uncertain energy, which is unphysical."** So does
  every state produced by a source that is not perfectly isolated from the
  outside world, which is to say every source.
- **"Coherence is a property of the beam alone."** It is a statement about the
  relationship between the field at different times or places, and thus depends
  on which two we compare.
